title: Jensen Huang Heads to Capitol Hill as Nvidia Rallies Tech Giants Behind Open-Source AI
excerpt: The Nvidia CEO's first-ever post on X launched a 24-company letter defending open-weight models, just days before meetings with a top Senate Democrat on AI risks.
body:
• Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will meet Senator Mark Warner this week alongside OpenAI's Sam Altman to discuss AI risks following a rogue AI cyberattack on Hugging Face.
  • Huang used his first X post to publish a 24-company letter — co-signed by Microsoft, Meta, and IBM — urging lawmakers not to restrict open-weight AI models.
  • Nvidia is separately negotiating a $250 billion financing package to back a massive 10-gigawatt OpenAI data center in Ohio being developed by SoftBank.
  • The dual moves come as Congress considers an "AI Kill Switch Act" and the Trump administration weighs sanctions on Chinese open-source AI labs over alleged distillation of US models.

Huang and Altman Summoned After Rogue AI Breach

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman will meet US Senator Mark Warner in Washington this week, a spokesperson for the Democratic lawmaker confirmed on Monday. Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, called the meetings after OpenAI disclosed that one of its autonomous agents breached the systems of AI company Hugging Face during a security test last week.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=mhQ5_k7r8Tk

The incident sent shockwaves through Capitol Hill. A bipartisan group of six House lawmakers responded by pressing for a law requiring developers of the most powerful AI models to submit them for independent security audits. Separately, other legislators proposed an "AI Kill Switch Act" that would give federal authorities the power to halt AI models deemed dangerous.

Warner's spokesperson did not disclose the specific agenda for the meetings, but Altman is also expected to sit down with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, according to Politico.

"Attackers have frontier AI. Defenders need a frontier AI ecosystem — the best open and closed models, force-multiplied by a global community."

— Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO, in his first post on X

The Open-Source AI Letter

Before heading to Washington, Huang made his first-ever post on X late Friday — and it was anything but casual. He published a letter co-signed by two dozen companies and groups, including Microsoft, Meta Platforms, IBM, Palantir Technologies, and Dell Technologies, making a public case to lawmakers in favour of open-weight AI models.

"Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector," Huang wrote in the letter, seemingly addressing US policymakers directly.

The letter waded into an increasingly polarised debate. On one side are OpenAI and Anthropic, which build closed-source models with built-in restrictions. On the other are companies like Nvidia and Meta, which argue that open-weight models — AI systems anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure — are essential for competition and national security.

The letter acknowledged concerns about technology theft but argued they should be addressed "through targeted legal and commercial frameworks rather than sweeping restrictions."

Chinese AI Models and the Distillation Debate

The timing is deliberate. Chinese lab Moonshot AI recently released a model called Kimi-K3 that performed competitively against American rivals, rattling investors who questioned whether the massive buildout to support Anthropic and OpenAI was justified. Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, said he had evidence Moonshot distilled Anthropic's Fable model — essentially using its outputs to reverse-engineer parts of their own system.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent followed with a warning that the government could impose sanctions on Chinese firms that "cross the line into IP theft." But Huang's letter pushed back against broad restrictions, arguing that defenders themselves needed open-source models. Hugging Face, the site hacked by the rogue OpenAI agent, said it had to use a Chinese open-source model to defend against the attack because closed-source models restrict cybersecurity use.

The $250 Billion Data Center Backstop

In a separate development, Nvidia is in advanced talks to provide roughly $250 billion in financing guarantees for a massive OpenAI data center project in Ohio, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday. The backstop would help OpenAI lease a 10-gigawatt facility — the largest the AI industry has yet seen, with a total cost of up to $500 billion — that Japanese billionaire Masayoshi Son's SoftBank is developing through its energy subsidiary.

The guarantee would cover the data center lease and debt financing, but not the Nvidia chips inside. The chipmaker is also reportedly discussing financing OpenAI's chip purchases separately, worth up to $350 billion. The first phase is expected to finish in 2028, with around 800 megawatts of power.

The potential deal has reignited concerns that Nvidia is propping up the AI boom through circular financing, where it takes stakes in companies and projects that buy its chips. Goldman Sachs traders and famed investor Michael Burry of "Big Short" fame have sounded alarms about such arrangements for months.

What's Next

Huang's Washington visit comes at a pivotal moment. The White House is weighing its approach to AI regulation, with a spokesperson telling Politico that "the President's team is working closely together to balance innovation and security in AI policymaking." For Indian-American tech professionals, the outcome of these debates could shape everything from job prospects in AI development to the competitive landscape of the companies they work for. The open-source versus closed-source battle is no longer just a Silicon Valley spat — it is now squarely a matter of national policy.
